findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify an atomic port-reservation mechanism (e.g., pass the already-bound listening socket fd directly to git daemon via --listen/--port with SO_REUSEPORT, or use a fixed loopback port protected by a file lock) so no TOCTOU window exists between port discovery and daemon bind.
evidence: 'Reserve a loopback port, then retry a socket connection every 100 ms for at most 30 seconds; startup failure raises immediately.'
No atomic hold-and-pass mechanism is described (e.g., SO_REUSEPORT, passing the listening fd directly to the daemon, or a fixed well-known port with an exclusion lock).
TOCTOU between socket close and daemon bind is a well-known portability/concurrency hazard in test fixtures.
findings.finding: The port-reservation step has an unaddressed TOCTOU race. The plan says 'Reserve a loopback port, then retry a socket connection every 100 ms for at most 30 seconds.' The canonical technique to discover a free port (bind a socket, read the port number, close the socket, then tell the daemon to listen on that port) leaves a window between the close and the daemon's bind during which another process or a parallel pytest-xdist worker can claim the port. The plan does not specify an atomic reservation mechanism, so the daemon startup can spuriously fail or bind to the wrong port in concurrent test runs, and the plan's retry-on-connection logic will then spend the full 30-second window before raising — silently masking the race.
findings.location: Real-Git fixture and protocol oracle — 'Reserve a loopback port, then retry a socket connection every 100 ms for at most 30 seconds; startup failure raises immediately.'
scenarios: Parallel pytest-xdist workers both discover the same free port, close their probe sockets, and both attempt to start git daemon on that port; one daemon fails to bind, the retry loop times out after 30 s, and the fixture raises — causing the entire integration test module to fail non-deterministically.

A single-process test run on a busy CI host where a system process grabs the ephemeral port between the probe close and daemon bind produces the same 30-second timeout, turning an intermittent infrastructure race into a hard block on the suite.
findings.suggested_fix: Bind a server socket to port 0, call getsockname() to get the assigned port, then pass --port=<N> to git daemon configured to bind the same address. Alternatively, use a fixed port (e.g., 9418 + worker_id) protected by a pytest-xdist worker-scoped file lock. Either eliminates the close→rebind race window.

findings.finding: The 'snapshot exact git count-objects -v before/after rebar verify-identity, fail if any line differs' guard mechanism will spuriously fail whenever foreground auto-gc fires during the verify-identity invocation. ADR 0051 (accepted, in-force) explicitly keeps gc.auto at the default ~6700-object threshold and sets gc.autoDetach=false so repacks run FOREGROUND under the write lock. git worktree add materializes tip blobs as loose objects; if the cumulative loose-object count in the shared object DB is near the threshold, a subsequent git commit (or the verify-identity scan itself touching internal objects) triggers foreground gc that repacks loose objects into a new pack file — changing the 'count' and 'size-pack' lines of git count-objects -v between the two snapshots even though verify-identity itself added zero promisor objects. The plan's guard cannot distinguish a real promisor leak from a gc-triggered repack, so it will produce spurious failures on CI. The codebase's own gc policy (ADR 0051, src/rebar/_commands/init.py:151-161, tests/interfaces/store/test_gc_config.py) confirms auto-gc is deliberately enabled and foreground — this is not a theoretical risk.
findings.location: Production guardrails section: 'snapshot exact git count-objects -v after materialization, run rebar verify-identity, snapshot again, and fail if any line differs'; AC lines for standalone_no_promisor, gerrit_no_promisor, standalone_identity_no_promisor, gerrit_identity_no_promisor
scenarios: Materialization fetches N loose blob objects for the tickets tip; combined with pre-existing loose objects in the shared object DB the count crosses gc.auto default (6700); foreground gc fires during rebar verify-identity; before-snapshot shows N loose objects, after-snapshot shows 0 loose + 1 new pack — guard flags false promisor leak, CI fails.

On a CI runner with a larger pre-existing object count, even a small materialization tips the threshold; every run of the identity job fails the no-promisor check despite verify-identity being correct.
findings.suggested_fix: Instead of diffing raw git count-objects -v output, check only the count of promisor remote entries (git config --get-all remote.*.promisor | grep -c true) before and after, or verify that a sentinel blob known to be missing pre-materialization is still absent (git cat-file -e <missing-blob-sha> exits non-zero) after verify-identity completes. Both checks are immune to gc-driven repack events.

findings.finding: The `pre_materialization_pack_guard` AC states it 'rejects an unfiltered all-history pack above 131072 KiB and accepts blobless below 102400 KiB,' but the Production guardrails section assigns these two limits to different jobs and lifecycle phases: 102400 KiB is the standalone verify-identity checkout limit (before any tickets worktree exists) and 131072 KiB is the Gerrit post-materialization limit. A test named 'pre_materialization' that uses 131072 KiB as its rejection threshold contradicts the guardrails section, which reserves 131072 KiB for a post-materialization context. An implementer reading both sections will be uncertain which guard the integration test is exercising and whether the fixture correctly represents the standalone (102400 KiB) pre-materialization scenario or the Gerrit (131072 KiB) post-materialization scenario.
findings.location: Production guardrails section vs. AC `pre_materialization_pack_guard` / tests/integration/test_ci_tickets_partial_clone.py
findings.suggested_fix: Rename/split the AC so one sub-case is labeled 'standalone_pre_materialization_pack_guard' asserting reject > 131072 KiB and accept < 102400 KiB (the stricter standalone limit), and another is 'gerrit_post_materialization_pack_guard' asserting reject > 131072 KiB and accept < 131072 KiB after worktree materialization. Annotate each numeric constant with the env-var name it mirrors (REBAR_CHECKOUT_PACK_LIMIT_KIB=102400 and REBAR_TICKETS_PACK_LIMIT_KIB=131072).

findings.finding: The plan requires tests to assert a 'capability packet advertising filter' and a 'client-to-server packet matching packet: followed by any non-space actor ending in >, then exact content filter blob:none', but nowhere names the Git mechanism that produces protocol-level packet traces. The standard mechanism is the `GIT_TRACE_PACKET` environment variable (or `GIT_TRACE2` event log). Without specifying how to capture these packets, the three protocol-oracle ACs (`named_origin_filter`, `direct_depth_filter`, `direct_full_filter`) and their capability/request regex assertions cannot be implemented by an executor — they have no signal to parse.
findings.location: Real-Git fixture and protocol oracle section: 'Capture packet traces for plain named-origin inheritance, direct URL with --depth=1 --filter=blob:none, and direct URL full-history with --filter=blob:none. findings.suggested_fix: In the 'Real-Git fixture and protocol oracle' section, add: 'Set `GIT_TRACE_PACKET=<tmpfile>` in the environment of the `git fetch`/`git clone` subprocess; after the call, read `<tmpfile>` and apply the capability/request regex. findings.finding: The push-retry-loop git fetches inside .tickets-tracker worktrees are unenumerated consumers of the filter inheritance behavior. reconcile-bridge.yml has a 'git fetch origin +tickets:refs/remotes/origin/tickets' at ~line 300 inside the Commit step's .tickets-tracker context, and reconcile-bridge-canary.yml has equivalent fetches at lines 431 and 446 in its Flush step. findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Tie every GIT_TRACE_PACKET file path to pytest's `tmp_path` or `tmp_path_factory` fixture (or explicitly delete it in the test's teardown) so trace files are retired automatically after each test.
evidence: 'Set GIT_TRACE_PACKET=<unique tmp trace file> in each git subprocess environment.'
The fixture cleanup section specifies only daemon process teardown: 'use yield/finally and always terminate()+wait(timeout=5), then kill()+wait()'. No mention of trace file deletion.

Trace files can be tens of MB each (full Git packet logs); with three separate captures mandated ('Capture separate packet traces for plain named-origin inheritance, direct URL with --depth=1 --filter=blob:none, and direct URL full-history') they accumulate on every test run.
findings.finding: The GIT_TRACE_PACKET temporary trace files have no specified RETIRE/cleanup path. The plan says 'Set GIT_TRACE_PACKET=<unique tmp trace file> in each git subprocess environment' and requires post-run regex assertions against those files, but never states who deletes them or how they are scoped. If they are created via tempfile.mkstemp or a similar ad-hoc call rather than pytest's tmp_path fixture, they accumulate in /tmp (or the OS temp dir) across test runs without ever being cleaned up.
findings.location: Real-Git fixture and protocol oracle — 'Set GIT_TRACE_PACKET=<unique tmp trace file> in each git subprocess environment.'
scenarios: On a long-running developer workstation where the integration suite is executed repeatedly, trace files accumulate in /tmp indefinitely, eventually filling the temp partition and causing unrelated processes to fail.

On a macOS runner where /tmp is a RAM-backed APFS volume, repeated CI runs without cleanup gradually consume available memory through tmpfs accumulation, producing OOM-adjacent failures with no obvious connection to the git tests.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass tmp_path (or tmp_path_factory.mktemp('traces')) into the helper that constructs the subprocess environment, and set GIT_TRACE_PACKET=str(tmp_path / 'packet_trace_<unique_id>.log'). pytest will delete the directory tree after the session.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Declare a minimum Git version requirement (e.g. skip or xfail below git 2.28 where protocol v2 filter support is stable) and add a Git version probe at fixture setup time so protocol oracle test failures produce a clear 'Git version X does not emit the expected packet format' diagnostic rather than a silent regex non-match.
evidence: Plan text: 'A Git 2.55 probe observed packet: fetch> filter blob:none for fetch and packet: clone> filter blob:none for clone.'

GIT_TRACE_PACKET output is an implementation detail of pkt-line.c whose format (the actor label prefix) is not part of any stable API contract and has changed across Git versions (e.g., 'git<' in ls-remote contexts vs 'fetch>' in fetch contexts as observed in multiple real traces).
GitHub-hosted ubuntu-latest runners ship a specific Git version that may differ from 2.55; the plan does not declare a minimum Git version requirement for the integration test fixture.

The regex 'packet:\s+\S+>\s+filter blob:none$' correctly avoids hard-coding the actor, but if the packet trace format or filter line format changed between the CI runner's Git version and 2.55, the test could produce false negatives without clear diagnostic output.
findings.finding: The plan makes a version-pinned empirical capability assertion ('A Git 2.55 probe observed packet: clone> filter blob:none for clone and packet: fetch> filter blob:none for fetch') without specifying the minimum Git version required on CI runners for this packet-label shape to be observable, leaving test reliability unverified across the Git versions GitHub-hosted runners actually ship.
findings.location: Real-Git fixture and protocol oracle section: 'A Git 2.55 probe observed packet: fetch> filter blob:none for fetch and packet: clone> filter blob:none for clone. Tests must not hard-code the actor label.'
scenarios: If ubuntu-latest ships Git 2.43 and the filter packet line is formatted differently than in 2.55, the protocol oracle test produces no match and the test fails with a confusing assertion error rather than a clear version-mismatch skip.

A future runner upgrade silently changes the Git version, and the packet trace regex stops matching, causing the integration test to fail with no indication that the underlying filter negotiation is actually working correctly.

findings.finding: The plan provides no positive rationale for choosing blob:none over blob:limit=1m. The session_log (comment 1/3) measured blob:limit=1m at 72.1 MiB / 13.2s versus blob:none at 68.7 MiB / 14.3s — the two are functionally equivalent on this workload. Without a stated reason for preferring blob:none (e.g., no size-tuning needed, semantically clean for a commit-graph-only use case, or avoidance of per-object size comparisons on every lazy fetch), an implementer has no principled basis to resist a future suggestion to switch to blob:limit=1m or to explain the choice if questioned.
findings.location: Plan section: 'Scope and mechanisms — Add the published actions/checkout v7 filter input'; 'Never use filter: tree:0' (negative rationale given) but no equivalent positive rationale for blob:none over blob:limit=1m
scenarios: A future implementer or reviewer proposes blob:limit=1m as 'essentially the same', citing the session_log numbers; no plan text exists to explain why blob:none was chosen.
findings.suggested_fix: Add to the Scope and mechanisms section: 'blob:none is chosen over blob:limit=1m (measured at 72.1 MiB — nearly identical) because it requires no size threshold to maintain and is semantically correct: only the commit graph and trees are needed; blobs are fetched on demand only during worktree materialization.'
